title: RBI Governor Defends Early FCNR(B) Closure as Dollar Inflows Hit $80 Billion
excerpt: Sanjay Malhotra calls the early window shutdown a calibrated, data-driven decision as NRI deposit inflows shatter the 2013 record and shore up India's balance of payments.
body:
• RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra expects at least $80 billion in inflows through three subsidized swap schemes opened in June, calling the early FCNR(B) window closure a \"data-driven\" decision
  • Banks have mobilized approximately $32 billion so far, mostly through FCNR(B) deposits, shattering the 2013 record of $26 billion
  • The RBI dismissed concerns about deposit recirculation and said the decision to close the window early was made \"from a position of strength\"

RBI Defends Early FCNR(B) Window Closure

Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra has defended the central bank's decision to close the discounted swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits by non-resident Indians earlier than planned, calling it a \"well-thought-out, calibrated, prudent and data-driven response to the evolving situation.\"

In an interview with the Financial Express published on Thursday, Malhotra said the RBI expects at least $80 billion in total inflows across all three subsidized swap schemes it opened in June to bolster foreign exchange reserves, according to Reuters.

\"This reflects the strong macroeconomic fundamentals of our country and would also further strengthen our balance of payments,\" Malhotra told the newspaper.

What Are FCNR(B) Deposits?

Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Banks) deposits—commonly called FCNR(B)—are fixed-term deposits that NRIs can hold in foreign currencies (typically US dollars, euros, or British pounds) at Indian banks. Unlike regular NRE or NRO accounts, FCNR(B) deposits shield holders from exchange-rate risk since both principal and interest are denominated in the foreign currency.

In June, the RBI opened a special window offering concessional swap rates to banks accepting these deposits, effectively making it cheaper for Indian banks to attract dollar funds from overseas Indians. The RBI bears the hedging cost, incentivizing banks to offer higher interest rates to NRI depositors.

Record-Breaking Inflows

Banks have mobilized nearly $32 billion so far, mostly through FCNR(B) deposits. That figure already surpasses the previous record FCNR drive in 2013, which raised $26 billion over a much longer period, according to Outlook Business. State Bank of India research estimates total FCNR(B) collections could reach $65–70 billion, with combined inflows across all three channels potentially hitting $80–85 billion.

\"Flows have been stronger than we expected and even stronger than what most market participants expected.\"

— Sanjay Malhotra, RBI Governor

Last week, the RBI decided to close the FCNR(B) swap window ahead of its original September 30 deadline. Malhotra said the decision was made \"from a position of strength,\" dismissing speculation that the early closure signaled any underlying weakness.

Addressing Recirculation Concerns

One concern raised by market participants was whether existing NRI deposits were simply being recycled into the new scheme to capture higher interest rates rather than representing fresh dollar inflows. Malhotra dismissed this directly.

\"We do not find any prima facie evidence of recirculation of the existing deposits, in whatever form, to be of any significance or concern,\" he told the Hindu BusinessLine in a related interview.

The governor also addressed questions about the RBI's balance-sheet exposure from bearing the hedging cost on potentially $50–60 billion in FCNR(B) inflows. \"It is not something which should be a matter of concern because we have a foolproof system of insuring ourselves. Whatever dollars we get, the excess foreign currency is invested in foreign assets. The risk, therefore, is not there,\" he said.

What This Means for NRI Depositors

For NRIs who already moved money into FCNR(B) deposits under the concessional window, their deposits remain locked in at the favorable rates for the full term. The early closure means new deposits will no longer benefit from the subsidized swap rates, but existing commitments are unaffected.

The broader impact on India's external position is significant. SBI Research estimates the measures could lift India's FY27 balance of payments surplus to over $50 billion, with the current account deficit contained at around 1%. Government securities have also attracted over $7 billion in foreign inflows since the June 5 policy announcements.

Malhotra reiterated that the RBI's exchange-rate policy remains unchanged: the rupee is market-determined, with intervention limited to curbing excessive volatility and speculative activity. \"Our policy on intervention remains the same,\" he said. The RBI's net forward forex position remains \"very manageable,\" according to the governor.
